name: Hana Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a ceramic tile kiln. My vocational certificate taught kiln settings, but the best part is pulling a cooled sample whose glaze has come out even. Cleaning glaze dust from a jammed conveyor after a long hot shift is less lovely.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a delivery van and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The kiln pay is low for an experienced operator, we have about three weeks saved, and there are few similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to explain fault-code wording, but I check the manual before changing the kiln setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the tile crew that AI can make a tidy heat log, but it cannot feel whether a glaze has bubbled. We still need to pull samples after the kiln cools. My father taught me to look twice before blaming a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kiln wage is below what other operators earn, our mortgage takes a lot, and we have about three weeks of expenses saved. My partner drives a delivery van and the hours change with orders. Few other tile plants are near us, so ordinary bills worry me even if AI amounts to little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting kiln speed and checking tiles after cooling. I use an AI app daily to explain unfamiliar fault-code wording, then compare it with the machine manual before changing a setting. On Saturday I'll take the offered paid overtime to clear the school-uniform bill, if orders hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, though the small AI change doesn't frighten me. A hot tile has to cool before anybody calls it good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a tile disagree with the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the log said a burner had held its temperature, but the sample tile had a pinhole glaze. I held the pallet and checked the burner with maintenance. A neat kiln log cannot make a pinholed tile sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one extra shift cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children's uniforms came out of this month's food margin, and my partner's delivery hours were shorter. I can cover it with one extra paid shift if the plant offers it. I cannot treat a promised shift as money already in our account.

say: A **heat log** cannot prove a glazed tile is sound after cooling.
I would tell our crew to **inspect samples** before a pallet leaves.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and lower kiln wage leave little room for bills.
My partner’s changing **delivery hours** make the mortgage feel exposed already.
do: **Keep** setting kiln speed and checking cooled sample tiles.
**Verify** daily AI fault explanations against the manual before changing settings.
feel: **Anxious** about existing low wages and household bills.
S0.quote: A neat kiln log cannot make a pinholed tile sound.
fieldNote: Hana **uses AI daily** for fault wording but treats cooled tiles and manual checks as evidence.
The **uniform bill** is an existing expense; an offered overtime shift would pay it, not create savings.

steps.text: Keep setting tile kiln and inspect cooled samples

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may buy clay and plan the kiln batches before robots move hot tiles. If management uses it to squeeze breaks, I would ask for the actual rota. A family cannot eat a more efficient spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to pick up a new panel, and the AI app already helps me read alarms. Still, a revised schedule could remove paid changeover time. With three weeks saved, one short wage would hurt us even if the kiln itself stays manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor to show the paid changeover minutes on next month's rota. If the plant offers a real paid place on its new kiln-control course with a trainer and cool practice tiles, I'll attend. I'll use the AI app to practise reading the panel guide after my shift, checking each answer against the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid minutes, but interested in the controls. The rota matters more than a sales presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the kiln course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the trainer to show what happens when a tile jams at the kiln exit. I would stop the belt, let the area cool and practise the restart on a training load. A kiln-control video alone is not safe instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can training fit school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can collect the children on the early delivery days, but not every day. A course scheduled at school pickup would need paid release at a different hour. I'd check the offered timetable before saying yes.

say: **AI planning** may change clay orders before robots move kiln tiles.
I would ask for the **paid changeover rota** before accepting a faster target.
think: I can learn **new controls** but cannot absorb one short wage.
Our **thin savings** leave no room for unpaid course time.
do: **Ask** supervisor for actual paid changeover minutes.
**Attend** offered paid trainer-led kiln course if safety and pickup schedule fit.
**Practise** AI panel-guide prompts and verify answers against the manual.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced paid time, despite interest in the controls.
S1.quote: A kiln-control video alone is not safe instruction.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive habits** include daily AI use and deliberate practice on a new panel guide.
Real **training participation** requires an offered paid place, safe instruction and a schedule compatible with school pickup.

steps.text: Check next paid kiln changeover rota with supervisor
Attend kiln-control course if paid safe place and pickup fit
Practise AI panel-guide prompts and verify against manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family thinking AI could plan every tile order by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could stack and inspect the kiln output. I would not argue that a familiar face guarantees a shift. I'd ask what paid work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the hands-on work. I expect our kiln crew could be cut hard, and my partner's variable delivery wage would not cover two children and the mortgage alone. Three weeks saved disappears quickly; I am already awake some nights counting bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the plant for a written robot timetable and remaining paid roles. If it offers a funded course with paid time, guarded practice and a genuine kiln-maintenance place, I'll enrol. If my shifts are cut, I'll apply for posted local warehouse or tile-factory jobs with safe duties, regular pay enough for the mortgage, and workable school hours; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local maintenance work under those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can learn a new control, but I cannot train my mortgage to wait three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe maintenance practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice needs a stopped conveyor, a cooled tile load and a proper lock on the burner. I'd ask the trainer to watch me test each step. I don't want a certificate earned from a screen while the hot line keeps running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge another vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse fallback is only if it posts a real vacancy. Most nearby jobs are not tile jobs, and the base wage has to cover our bills without assuming overtime. My partner and I would compare its shift with the children's school hours before I apply.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may plan tile orders before capable robots reach the kiln around 2031.
I would seek a **written plant plan** for paid roles before relying on promises.
think: At **48**, major kiln-hour cuts could leave one variable delivery wage.
Our **three-week reserve** would barely bridge a mortgage payment.
do: **Ask** plant for a robot timetable and remaining paid roles.
**Enrol** if funded paid guarded kiln-maintenance place offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local roles if hours cut and base pay and school hours fit.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless bill counting.
S2.quote: I can learn a new control, but I cannot train my mortgage to wait three months.
fieldNote: She expects **major kiln-hour loss** and already lies awake over a three-week household reserve.
Her **two applications** are distinct: immediate fallback if cut and qualified maintenance after an offered funded practical course.

steps.text: Ask plant for written robot timetable and remaining paid roles
Enrol in kiln maintenance if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply to posted safe local warehouse/tile jobs if cut, pay and school hours fit
Apply to posted safe local maintenance if qualified, shifts cut, pay and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years to thinking AI in 2031 is time to learn a kiln's new controls before capable robots handle tiles around 2034. We should ask for paid practical seats while we still have paid shifts. A kiln-inspection brochure is no paid course seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when physical robots arrive. I can practise a guarded inspection role, but the plant may never offer one, and my partner's delivery hours may change first. The mortgage still runs each month. I want a useful qualification, not a gamble with food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep running the kiln and put new money from any offered extra paid shift into a bill reserve after school costs. I'll ask the supervisor for the exact fee, paid-release and practical place terms of the tile-inspection certificate. If a funded paid guarded place is offered, I'll enrol; once qualified, if hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local inspection work with enough regular pay and workable school hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to pace it. I can ask for the course terms before moving our family's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the inspection test cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should make me spot pinholes and a hairline crack on cooled tiles, then stop a bad pallet. I would not inspect a moving hot stack with my hands. That is what the paid practice must cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a job posting say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any posting must name the base wage and the shift start. If the hours clash with school pickup and the delivery round, we need paid child care or a different shift. I would not apply on a title alone.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes tile planning before capable robots handle kiln output around 2034.
A real **paid course seat** matters more than a training brochure.
think: At **51**, I might qualify for inspection if an actual place opens.
The **mortgage** still needs regular wages despite a longer warning.
do: **Save** new wages from offered extra shifts after school costs.
**Enrol** in tile inspection if fees and paid guarded practice are covered.
**Apply** to posted safe local inspection jobs if qualified, hours cut and pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, with more time to verify course terms.
S3.quote: A kiln-inspection brochure is no paid course seat.
fieldNote: Her **new reserve deposits** require actual extra paid shifts; the course enquiry alone does not count as enrolment.
An **inspection application** follows qualification and hour cuts, with safe local posting, adequate base pay and workable school hours.

steps.text: Save new money from offered extra kiln shifts after school costs
Enrol in tile inspection if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours cut, pay and school hours fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 could plan kiln batches, then capable robots around 2039 could handle and inspect tiles. Ten years gives a family time to teach skills at home and make decisions together. I won't call a machine a family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots can do the physical kiln work. The children may be grown, but I cannot count on an empty mortgage or a secure delivery route for my partner. Our three weeks saved now makes every new plan depend on paid work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the kiln job and save new money from any offered extra paid shifts once bills are covered. I'll ask my uncle, who repairs conveyors, whether his workshop has a real paid apprenticeship with guarded practice. If a funded place and schedule that fits our family are offered, I'll take it; once qualified, if kiln hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local repair work only if regular pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's little cushion, although the long warning gives us choices. I would feel less rushed about choosing a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can your uncle really arrange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle can tell me whether a place has wages, a trainer and practice on a locked conveyor. A paid conveyor apprenticeship needs a trainer and guarded practice; my uncle cannot reserve a seat for me. I would ask for the written offer myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to trace a belt fault, isolate the power and restart on a test load with the trainer watching. If the course skips the guarded practice, I would keep the kiln wage and look for another offered place.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes tile planning before robots handle kiln output around 2039.
A **family apprenticeship** helps only when it offers wages, a trainer and safe practice.
think: At **56**, I may still need the kiln wage for household bills.
Our current **three-week reserve** makes a paid place essential.
do: **Save** new money from offered paid shifts after bills.
**Attend** conveyor apprenticeship if funded paid guarded place and family schedule fit.
**Apply** to posted safe local repair work if qualified, kiln hours cut and pay sufficient.
feel: **Anxious** about current thin savings while seeing time to prepare.
S4.quote: A paid conveyor apprenticeship needs a trainer and guarded practice; my uncle cannot reserve a seat for me.
fieldNote: Her **traditional outlook** puts family craft knowledge beside offered paid instruction, without assuming a relative can hire her.
The **repair application** depends on qualification, kiln-hour cuts and a real safe local opening with sufficient base pay.

steps.text: Save new wages from offered extra kiln shifts after bills
Ask conveyor-repair uncle about real paid guarded apprenticeship
Attend conveyor apprenticeship if funded paid guarded place and schedule fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut our kiln crew before I can earn a new certificate. A written paid-role plan, an offered funded practical place and posted safe local work at enough regular pay would help. I would still ask my family what hours we could manage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs a pallet of tiles after a robot sorts it. A cracked tile does not become sound because a machine printed a neat label.

headlineQuote: A cracked tile does not become sound because a machine printed a neat label.
portrait: **Hana**, 43, operates a ceramic tile kiln with a vocational certificate and daily AI use for fault wording.
She and her delivery-driver partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage on low pay with three weeks saved.
Her **traditional outlook** values family apprenticeship and paid work, while she quickly learns useful machine controls.
Fast robots make her **alarmed** about major kiln-hour loss; extra earned wages, safe training and real local vacancies guide her plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable kiln robots around 2031 and cut the paid shifts supporting her family.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid-role plan**, offered funded practical training and posted safe local jobs with sufficient regular pay would help.
